preamble: Arabic reflex of the Proto-Semitic emphatic interdental. *ṯ̣, reconstructed as an ejective [θʼ], survives as a separate phoneme in Arabic ẓāʾ ظ, a velarized [ðˠ] in Classical Arabic and a pharyngealized [ðˤ] in Modern Standard Arabic (Wikipedia, Ẓāʾ). Between the two ends, glottalization gives way to pharyngealization and the fricative is voiced. In Hebrew, Akkadian and Geʽez *ṯ̣ merged with *ṣ instead, and in Aramaic and Soqotri it became ṭ. The Proto-Semitic value is a reconstruction: the emphatics are generally reconstructed as glottalized, i.e. ejective (Cantineau 1952; Kogan 2011: 61, cited by Wikipedia), but some reconstructions give *ṯ̣ itself as [θˤ] or [ðˤ] (Wikipedia, Ẓāʾ), 'maximal' accounts make it an affricate [tθʼ] (Wikipedia, Proto-Semitic language), and Militarev's Semitic etymology gives *č̣ as an alternative in the roots for 'nail' and 'to be thirsty'. This entry follows the [θʼ] of Wikipedia's Proto-Semitic consonant table. The Harsusi entry is tentative: Al Balushi (2019: 18, cited by Wikipedia) lists /ðˤ/ in the Harsusi consonant table, but the Modern South Arabian counterpart of ظ is also given as ejective [θʼ ~ ðʼ] (Wikipedia, Modern South Arabian), and Mehri emphatics may also be pharyngealized (Watson & Bellem 2011, cited by Wikipedia), being ejective before a pause and pharyngealized elsewhere according to Wikipedia's Mehri article. Within Arabic, ẓāʾ later merged with ḍād in most vernaculars, and in inherited words of Egyptian, Levantine, Hijazi and Moroccan Arabic it became a stop [dˤ].
